record.paper_title: Achievement sets – current results and open problems
record.original_question: For every geometric sequence (q^n)_{n∈ℕ} with q in (1/2, 1), does there exist a subsequence (q^{n_k})_{k∈ℕ} whose achievement set is a Cantorval?

evidence.quote: Does every geometric sequence (q^n)n∈ℕ with q ∈ (1/2, 1) contain a subsequence (q^nk)k∈ℕ such that E(q^nk) is a Cantorval?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be an absolutely summable sequence of positive real numbers. Its achievement set (or subsum set) is
$$E((a_n)) = \Big\{\sum_{n\in A} a_n : A \subseteq \mathbb{N}\Big\}.$$
By a classical theorem of Kakeya–Guthrie–Nymann, for any such sequence $E((a_n))$ is one of the following: a finite set, a finite union of non-degenerate closed intervals, a set homeomorphic to the Cantor ternary set, or a Cantorval. Here a Cantorval (more precisely an $\mathcal{M}$-Cantorval) is a non-empty compact subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $C$ is the closure of its interior, both endpoints of every non-degenerate component of $C$ are accumulation points of degenerate (one-point) components of $C$, and $C$ has uncountably many connected components.

Question: For every real number $q \in (1/2, 1)$, does there exist a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers $(n_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that the achievement set $E\big((q^{n_k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\big)$ is a Cantorval?
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and research articles on achievement sets (subsum sets) explicitly list this question as open. Even restricted to geometric sequences with ratio q ∈ (1/2, 1), it is reported that whether every such q admits a subsequence with Cantorval achievement set is unknown, and the problem is featured in current open-problem lists on the topic.

status_evidence.title: Achievement sets – current results and open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Lists as an open problem whether every geometric sequence (q^n) with q ∈ (1/2,1) contains a subsequence whose achievement set is a Cantorval.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is presented as currently open.

status_evidence.title: On a new condition implying that an achievement set is a Cantorval and its applications
status_evidence.snippet: Develops new sufficient conditions for achievement sets to be Cantorvals; relevant to but does not resolve the geometric subsequence question.
status_evidence.claim: Active recent research on conditions for Cantorval achievement sets, without settling the geometric subsequence question.
